topics.title: Static charge and charging by rubbing

learn.hook: Ever felt a tiny zap when you pull off a woollen sweater on a dry December night in Delhi? That crackle is electrostatics in action.
points: Electrostatics is the study of forces, fields and potentials due to charges at rest.
Everyday static effects: sparks when removing synthetic clothes, a rubbed comb picking up paper bits, and lightning during thunderstorms.
Rubbing two suitable bodies charges both: a glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive, while amber or a plastic rod rubbed with fur or wool becomes negative.
There are only two kinds of charge. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Benjamin Franklin named them positive and negative.
Charging means transfer of electrons: the body that loses electrons becomes positive, the one that gains them becomes negative. Protons do not move.

example.q: A glass rod is rubbed with silk and then brought near a second glass rod that was also rubbed with silk. What happens, and why?
steps: Rubbing with silk pulls electrons off glass, so each glass rod is positively charged.
Both rods carry the same kind of charge.
example.answer: The rods repel each other, because both carry positive charge.

learn.reallife: On a dry winter day, petrol tankers on Indian highways drag a metal chain or use an earthing strip so that static charge built up by friction leaks to the ground instead of sparking near fuel.

Electrons moved from the glass to the silk
Electrons moved from the silk to the glass

Like charges repel and unlike charges attract

neutral, because fur is an insulator
positively charged, with twice the magnitude

Charge is conserved: fur gets an equal positive charge

quiz.q: A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall. Which everyday effect is of the same kind?
options: A bulb glowing when a switch is closed
A comb run through dry hair attracting bits of paper
Water boiling in an electric kettle
quiz.explain: Both are static electricity effects from charges produced by friction.

A comb run through dry hair is also charged by friction and attracts paper
Answer: A comb run through dry hair attracting bits of paper

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

R: an electron carries negative charge – true

quiz.explain: X attracts positive Z, so X is negative. Y repels X, so Y has the same sign as X: negative.
steps: X attracts positive Z, so X is negative
Y repels X, so Y is like X

quiz.q: Why do you get a small shock when touching a metal door handle after walking on a nylon carpet in dry weather?
options: The handle stores current from the mains
Dry air conducts electricity very well
Your body gathers charge by friction and discharges through the handle
quiz.explain: Friction between shoes and carpet transfers electrons; touching a conductor lets the charge rush out as a small spark. Dry air lets charge build up instead of leaking away.
steps: Walking on nylon transfers electrons by friction; dry air lets charge build up
Touching a metal conductor lets the charge rush out as a spark
Answer: Your body gathers charge by friction and discharges through the handle
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shock comes from the mains supply

learn.hook: Why does a metal spoon rubbed on wool show no charge, while a plastic scale does? The answer is where the charge can go.
points: Conductors let charge move freely through them: metals, the human body and the earth are examples.
Insulators such as glass, plastic, rubber and dry wood resist the flow of charge, so charge placed on them stays where it was put.
Charge given to a conductor spreads over its whole outer surface at once; a metal held in the hand loses its charge to earth through the body.
Semiconductors (like silicon and germanium) have conduction in between conductors and insulators.

A gold-leaf electroscope detects charge: charge on the cap spreads to the two leaves, which repel and diverge. A point charge is a charged body whose size is tiny compared with the distances involved.

example.q: Why must you hold a metal rod with a plastic handle if you want to charge it by rubbing?
steps: A metal is a conductor, so charge spreads over it freely.
Held in bare hands, the charge would flow through your body to the earth.
The plastic handle is an insulator and blocks this leakage.
example.answer: The insulating handle stops the charge from leaking to earth through the body, so the metal stays charged.

learn.reallife: Electricians in India use rubber gloves and insulated screwdrivers because rubber and plastic are insulators, while the human body, like any conductor, would carry charge to the earth.

Both leaves get the same kind of charge and repel
quiz.explain: The charge spreads to both leaves, giving them like charges, so they repel.

Like charges repel, so they diverge

options: Charge spreads over the metal surface but stays at the spot on the glass
Charge stays at the spot on both
Charge spreads through the glass but not the metal

In an insulator they cannot move, so they stay where put

Only when it has charge of exactly 1 C
quiz.explain: A point charge is an idealisation; it works when the body's size is negligible compared with separations.
steps: A point charge is an idealisation
It works when the body's size is tiny compared with the distances involved
Answer: When its size is very small compared with the distances being considered

A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true

R: body and earth are conductors – true

measure electric current in a circuit

So divergence shows that a body is charged

learn.hook: A bank balance and electric charge have something in common: both add up with plus and minus signs, and neither can be made from nothing.
points: Additivity: the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of all its charges. Charge is a scalar. For example, +2q, -3q and +5q give +4q.
Conservation: charge is never created or destroyed in an isolated system; it is only transferred. This holds even in nuclear processes and pair production.
Quantisation: every free charge is an integer multiple of the basic charge, q = ne, where e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and n is an integer.
The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C). Practical sub-units are µC (10⁻⁶ C) and nC (10⁻⁹ C).
Even 1 µC contains about 10¹³ electronic charges, so at the large scale quantisation is unnoticeable and charge is treated as continuous.

example.q: How many electrons must be removed from a neutral body to give it a charge of +3.2 µC? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

learn.reallife: In ISRO's satellites, engineers worry about spacecraft charging: electrons hitting the craft in orbit add up (additivity) and can build large voltages, so surfaces are designed to share and leak charge safely.

quiz.q: Three charges +4 µC, -7 µC and +1 µC are placed in a box. What is the total charge in the box (in µC)?
quiz.explain: Charge is additive and scalar, so add with signs: 4 - 7 + 1 = -2 µC.

quiz.q: How many electrons make up a charge of -8 × 10⁻¹⁸ C? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

quiz.q: Which of these cannot be the charge on an isolated body? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.explain: 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is 1.5e, not a whole-number multiple of e, so it breaks quantisation.
steps: Quantisation: q = ne with n a whole number
quiz.mistake: Forgets that n must be an integer

quiz.q: A current of electrons removes 10¹² electrons per second from a neutral body. How long (in seconds) will it take for the body to gain a charge of +1.6 µC? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.explain: Charge gained per second = 10¹² × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ C. Time = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ / 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ = 10 s.
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong power of ten for µ

quiz.q: In the decay of a free neutron, it changes into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. Which property of charge does this obey?
options: Quantisation only, since charge is lost
Charge is created in nuclear processes
quiz.explain: The total charge before (zero) equals the total after: +e - e + 0 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks charge conservation fails in nuclear reactions

quiz.q: Why is quantisation of charge ignored when we deal with charges of a few microcoulombs?
options: Quantisation is only true for protons
Each microcoulomb contains about 10¹³ electronic charges, so charge looks continuous
The value of e changes at large scale
quiz.explain: Steps of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C are far too small to notice in a total of 10⁻⁶ C.
steps: Steps of one e are far too small to notice
Answer: Each microcoulomb contains about 10¹³ electronic charges, so charge looks continuous
quiz.mistake: Thinks quantisation is false at large scale rather than unnoticeable

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Charge is a scalar quantity. Reason (R): Charges add algebraically, taking their signs into account, not by direction. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Signs on charge mean positive or negative, not direction; addition is algebraic, so charge is a scalar.
steps: A: charge is a scalar – true
R: charges add algebraically with signs, not by direction – true
Algebraic (not vector) addition is why charge is scalar, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Treats the sign of charge as a direction

quiz.q: A neutral comb gains 5 × 10¹² electrons when it is run through hair. What is its charge, in µC? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.explain: q = -ne = -5 × 10¹² × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = -8 × 10⁻⁷ C = -0.8 µC. It is negative because electrons were gained.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign or the micro conversion

teach.ask: Gappu found a speck with charge 0.5e in a cartoon. 'Is that possible in real life?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Free charges always come in whole-number multiples of e, so 0.5e is cartoon physics!
teach.nudge: Close! What rule tells us which values of charge are allowed?

revise.summary: Charge is additive (a scalar), conserved in an isolated system and quantised as q = ne with e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Since 1 µC holds about 10¹³ electronic charges, large-scale charge looks continuous.
traps: A charge that is not a whole multiple of e is impossible
Don't give a positive sign to a body that gains electrons; it becomes negative

learn.hook: Double the distance between two charges and the force drops to a quarter. This inverse-square rule shapes everything from atoms to lightning.
points: Coulomb's law: the force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
F = (1/4πε₀) q₁q₂/r², with 1/4πε₀ = k ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻² (permittivity of free space).
Vector form: F₂₁ = k q₁q₂ r̂₂₁/r², where r̂₂₁ points from q₁ to q₂. The force is along the line joining the charges, and F₁₂ = -F₂₁ (Newton's third law).
1 coulomb is the charge that, placed 1 m from an equal charge in vacuum, repels it with a force of 9 × 10⁹ N.
If q₁q₂ > 0 the force is repulsive; if q₁q₂ < 0 it is attractive.

example.q: Two point charges of 2 µC and 3 µC are 30 cm apart in air. Find the force between them.

learn.reallife: Laser printers and photocopiers in every Indian office use Coulomb attraction: charged toner powder is pulled onto oppositely charged regions of a drum to form the letters.

Coulomb forces obey Newton's third law.
Coulomb's law in its simple form applies to any pair of large charged bodies at any distance.
It is exact for point charges; extended bodies close together need integration.
The value of k = 1/4πε₀ is about 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
This is the standard value in vacuum.

Unlike charges attract.

quiz.mistake: Uses r instead of r²

quiz.q: The force between two point charges is F. If the distance between them is tripled, the new force is
quiz.explain: F ∝ 1/r². Tripling r divides F by 3² = 9.
quiz.mistake: Uses an inverse rather than an inverse-square law

quiz.q: The force between two charges is 12 N. Each charge is doubled and the distance is also doubled. What is the new force (in N)?
quiz.explain: F ∝ q₁q₂/r²: (2 × 2)/2² = 1, so the force is unchanged.
quiz.mistake: Doubles for each change without squaring r

quiz.q: Two equal charges q placed 1 m apart in vacuum repel with a force of 9 × 10⁹ N. What is q (in C)?
quiz.explain: F = kq²/r² gives 9 × 10⁹ = 9 × 10⁹ q²/1, so q = 1 C. This is how 1 coulomb is defined from Coulomb's law.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that k already equals 9 × 10⁹

quiz.q: In the vector form F₂₁ = k q₁q₂ r̂₂₁/r², what does a negative value of q₁q₂ mean?
options: The force on q₂ points towards q₁ (attraction)
The force on q₂ points away from q₁ (repulsion)
The force is perpendicular to the line joining them
quiz.explain: r̂₂₁ points from q₁ to q₂. A negative product reverses it, so q₂ is pulled towards q₁.
steps: r̂₂₁ points from q₁ to q₂
If q₁q₂ < 0 the force on q₂ is along −r̂₂₁, i.e. towards q₁
Answer: The force on q₂ points towards q₁ (attraction)
quiz.mistake: Ignores the sign of the product when finding direction

quiz.q: Two small charged spheres attract with a force of 0.8 N. They are moved so the separation becomes half. What is the new force (in N)?
quiz.explain: Halving r makes F four times larger: 4 × 0.8 = 3.2 N.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the force instead of quadrupling it

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of ε₀, the permittivity of free space?
quiz.explain: From F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²), ε₀ = q₁q₂/(4πFr²), giving C²/(N m²).
quiz.mistake: Writes the unit of k instead of ε₀

quiz.q: Point charges +2 µC and -8 µC are 3 m apart in air. What is the magnitude of the force between them (in mN)?
quiz.explain: F = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 8 × 10⁻⁶ / 9 = 1.6 × 10⁻² N = 16 mN, and it is attractive.
quiz.mistake: Divides by r instead of r²

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'If I move two charged beads twice as far apart, does the push become half?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It is inverse square, so twice the distance means one quarter of the force. Thank you!
teach.nudge: Nearly there! How exactly does the force depend on the distance, and on the two charges?

learn.hook: A small fridge magnet beats the whole Earth's gravity. Electric forces are even more dramatic: between an electron and a proton, they win by about 10³⁹ times!
points: The electric force between an electron and a proton is about 2.4 × 10³⁹ times their gravitational attraction, so gravity is negligible in atomic physics.
Electric forces can attract or repel; gravity only attracts. Both are inverse-square, central forces.
Superposition principle: the force on a charge due to many charges is the vector sum of the forces due to each charge, each calculated as if the others were absent.
Symmetry shortcut: equal charges at the corners of a regular polygon (triangle, square, hexagon) exert zero net force on a charge at the centre.
For an equilateral triangle of equal charges q with side l, the net force on one corner charge is √3 kq²/l².

example.q: Equal charges q are at the three corners of an equilateral triangle. What is the net force on a charge Q placed at the centroid?
steps: Each corner is at the same distance from the centroid, so each force has the same size.
Three equal vectors 120° apart add to zero.

learn.reallife: Gravity runs the solar system, ISRO's orbits and cricket ball flight because large bodies are nearly neutral. Electric forces are so strong that even a tiny charge imbalance would overwhelm gravity.

Gravity does not depend on distance

Each pair: equal charges at equal distances push the centre charge in opposite directions
All forces cancel in pairs: net force = 0

quiz.q: Charges of +1 µC each sit at two corners of an equilateral triangle of side 30 cm. What is the magnitude of the net force on a +1 µC charge at the third corner (in N)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²; take √3 = 1.73)
quiz.explain: Each force is F = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹²/0.09 = 0.1 N. The angle between them is 60°, so the resultant is 2F cos 30° = √3F = 0.173 N.

quiz.q: The superposition principle states that the force on a charge due to a group of charges is
options: the algebraic sum of the magnitudes
the vector sum of the individual forces from each charge
the force due to the nearest charge only
the product of all individual forces
quiz.explain: Each charge acts independently, and forces add as vectors.
steps: Each charge acts as if the others were absent
Forces are vectors, so they add as vectors
Answer: the vector sum of the individual forces from each charge
quiz.mistake: Adds magnitudes without considering directions

quiz.q: Charges +q are at all four corners of a square, and a charge Q is at the centre. One corner charge is now replaced by -q. The net force on Q is due effectively to
options: no charge, so it is zero
only the -q charge, pointing away from it
four charges, pointing perpendicular to the diagonal
two charges of +q and -q at the same diagonal, so it points along that diagonal

topics.title: Electric field of a point charge

learn.hook: A charge changes the space around it, like a hot tawa that warms the air before you touch it. That changed space is the electric field.
points: Electric field E at a point = force per unit positive test charge: E = F/q₀ (q₀ very small so it does not disturb the source). Unit: N C⁻¹.
Field of a point charge Q: E = kQ/r² r̂, pointing radially outward for positive Q and inward for negative Q.
The field depends only on the source charge and position, not on the test charge. A charge q placed there feels F = qE.
Physical significance: the field acts as the middleman of the interaction. For time-dependent situations the field travels at a finite speed and carries energy and momentum (electromagnetic waves).
In a uniform field, an electron and a proton feel equal force eE but accelerations eE/m differ. The electron (much lighter) falls through the same distance far faster.

example.q: Find the electric field 3 m from a point charge of +9 nC in air.
steps: = 81/9 = 9 N C⁻¹, pointing away from the charge

learn.reallife: Fair-weather Earth has a downward electric field of about 100 N C⁻¹ near the ground. India's monsoon thunderclouds can push local fields above 10⁴–10⁵ N C⁻¹, which is when lightning starts.

A negative charge attracts a positive test charge towards itself

quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 instead of 4

teach.praise: Chirp! The field belongs to the source charge, and the test charge only measures it. Super!
teach.nudge: Good! Does the field depend on the test charge, or only on the source?

revise.summary: The electric field E = F/q₀ is force per unit positive test charge, independent of the test charge. A point charge gives E = kQ/r², radially outward for positive and inward for negative Q.

topics.title: Field of several charges and field lines

learn.hook: Weather maps show wind with arrows. Physicists draw electric fields the same way, with lines that tell direction at a glance and strength by their crowding.
points: Field of a system of charges: E = E₁ + E₂ + ... (vector sum of each charge's field, by superposition).
Between two like charges the fields oppose; a neutral point (E = 0) lies between them, nearer the smaller charge. Between unlike charges the fields add.
A field line is a curve whose tangent at any point gives the direction of E; closer lines mean a stronger field.
Properties: lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity); they are continuous, never cross, and do not form closed loops in electrostatics.
Patterns: radial lines for a single charge, lines bending apart with a neutral point for two equal like charges, and lines running from + to - for a dipole.

example.q: Charges +4 µC and +1 µC are 3 m apart. Where between them is the electric field zero?
steps: Let the point be x from the 4 µC charge.
example.answer: 2 m from the 4 µC charge (1 m from the 1 µC charge)

learn.reallife: When India's weather scientists study thunderclouds, they map the electric field just as you draw field lines: crowded lines near cloud bases warn of a coming lightning strike.

quiz.q: Why can two electric field lines never intersect?
options: At the crossing point the field would have two directions, which is impossible
Because field lines are always straight
Because lines can only exist near charges
quiz.explain: E has a single definite direction at each point, given by the tangent to the line.
steps: The tangent to a field line gives the direction of E
At a crossing there would be two tangents, i.e. two directions of E
E has one definite direction at each point

steps: Line density is proportional to field strength

bend away so that no line passes through the midpoint, which is a neutral point
are most crowded at the midpoint
quiz.explain: Lines from like charges repel each other's pattern; the fields cancel at the midpoint.
steps: Two equal positive charges: their fields cancel at the midpoint
Lines bend away and none passes through it; it is a neutral point
Answer: bend away so that no line passes through the midpoint, which is a neutral point

quiz.q: The electric field due to a system of point charges at a point is found by

adding the fields of each charge as vectors
taking the field of the largest charge
quiz.explain: Superposition applies to fields just as to forces.
steps: Superposition: each charge's field is found as if alone
E is a vector, so the fields add as vectors
Answer: adding the fields of each charge as vectors
quiz.mistake: Ignores directions while adding fields

revise.summary: The field of several charges is the vector sum of individual fields. Field lines start on positive and end on negative charges, never cross, form no closed loops and are denser where the field is stronger.
focus: Superposition of fields and neutral points
remember: Like charges: neutral point between, nearer smaller charge
Unlike charges: fields add between them
Lines never cross; closer lines = stronger field

Electrostatic field lines never form closed loops

learn.hook: Hold a ring under a monsoon shower: how much rain passes through depends on the rain's strength, the ring's size and its tilt. Electric flux works exactly the same way.
points: For a point charge, field lines spread over spheres of area 4πr², so lines per unit area fall as 1/r². This matches E ∝ 1/r² (the solid-angle picture of Coulomb's law).
Electric flux through a small area: Δφ = E·ΔS = E ΔS cosθ, where ΔS is the area vector, normal to the surface.
Flux is roughly the number of field lines crossing the surface. Unit: N m² C⁻¹ (also V m).
For a uniform field through a flat area S at angle θ between E and the normal: φ = ES cosθ. Maximum when the surface faces the field (θ = 0), zero when the field skims along it (θ = 90°).
For a closed surface the outward normal is taken as positive: outgoing lines count +, incoming lines count -.

example.q: A uniform field of 200 N C⁻¹ makes an angle of 60° with the normal to a flat area of 0.5 m². Find the flux.

learn.reallife: Solar panel installers in Rajasthan tilt panels to face the Sun because the energy collected, like flux, is greatest when the surface normal points along the incoming rays.

The lines get weaker and fade away
The charge loses lines with distance
Each line bends back towards the charge

flux that depends on the charge outside only
quiz.explain: Outward normals are positive by convention, so incoming field gives cos θ < 0.

An entering line makes θ > 90° with it, so cosθ < 0

the field makes 45° with the surface
the field is perpendicular to the surface (along its normal)
quiz.explain: cos θ is largest (1) when E is along the normal, i.e. perpendicular to the surface plane.

θ = 0 means E is along the normal, i.e. perpendicular to the surface
Answer: the field is perpendicular to the surface (along its normal)

revise.summary: Electric flux measures field lines through a surface: Δφ = E·ΔS = EΔS cosθ. For a uniform field through a flat area, φ = ES cosθ, maximum when E is along the normal and zero when E is parallel to the surface.

Don't use areas in cm²; convert to m²

learn.hook: A water molecule is a tiny dipole. That is why water dissolves salt, heats in a microwave and clings to a charged comb stream.
points: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges +q and -q separated by 2a. Dipole moment p = q × 2a, a vector pointing from -q to +q. Unit: C m.
Field on the axis at distance r from the centre (r ≫ a): E = 2p/(4πε₀r³), directed along p.
Field on the equatorial plane (r ≫ a): E = -p/(4πε₀r³), directed opposite to p.
At the same large distance, the axial field is twice the equatorial field.
A dipole's field falls as 1/r³, faster than the 1/r² of a single charge, because the fields of +q and -q nearly cancel far away.

example.q: A dipole has charges ±10 µC separated by 2 mm. Find the field on its axis 10 cm from the centre.
example.answer: 3.6 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, along the dipole moment

learn.reallife: Microwave ovens in Indian kitchens heat food by twisting water dipoles back and forth billions of times a second; the jostling molecules warm your dal.

from the negative charge to the positive charge

options: The dipole has more total charge

Far away, the fields of +q and -q nearly cancel, leaving a small difference
quiz.explain: The two charges are almost at the same place from far away; only their small separation leaves a net field.
steps: From far away +q and −q are almost at the same place

Answer: Far away, the fields of +q and -q nearly cancel, leaving a small difference

quiz.q: At a point on the equatorial plane of a dipole, the electric field is
options: perpendicular to the dipole axis, pointing away from the dipole

The remaining components point from the + side to the − side, i.e. along −p

quiz.q: At the same large distance r, what is the ratio of axial field to equatorial field magnitude for a short dipole?
quiz.explain: 2kp/r³ ÷ kp/r³ = 2.

teach.ask: Gappu sees '+q and -q close together' and asks: 'They cancel, so there is no field, right?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A dipole has zero net charge but still makes a field that falls as 1/r³. Twice as big on the axis!
teach.nudge: Good! Does the field vanish completely, and how does it change with distance?

revise.summary: An electric dipole is ±q separated by 2a with moment p = q × 2a from −q to +q. For r ≫ a, the axial field is 2kp/r³ along p and the equatorial field is kp/r³ opposite to p; dipole fields fall as 1/r³.
remember: p = q × 2a, from −q to +q; unit C m
traps: p points from − to +, not + to −
Dipole field ∝ 1/r³, not 1/r²

learn.hook: Run a plastic comb through dry hair and hold it near tiny paper bits. They leap up even though the paper was neutral. A dipole in a non-uniform field explains it.
points: An ideal (point) dipole: q → ∞ and 2a → 0 while p = q × 2a stays finite.
Polar molecules (H₂O, HCl) have a permanent dipole moment. Non-polar molecules (O₂, H₂, CO₂) have none, but an external field induces one by shifting their charges.
In a uniform field, the forces qE and -qE cancel, so the net force on a dipole is zero.
But the two forces form a couple: torque τ = p × E, magnitude τ = pE sinθ. It rotates p into line with E.
In a non-uniform field there is a net force too. A dipole aligned with E moves towards stronger field; that is why a charged comb attracts neutral paper (it first polarises it).

example.q: A dipole of moment 4 × 10⁻⁹ C m is at 30° to a uniform field of 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Find the torque.
example.answer: 1 × 10⁻⁴ N m, tending to align p with E

learn.reallife: At AIIMS and other hospitals, MRI is magnetic, but microwave diathermy used in physiotherapy relies on electric dipoles in tissue water rotating in an alternating field, warming deep muscles.

quiz.q: The torque on a dipole in a uniform field is maximum when the angle between p and E is
quiz.explain: sin θ is largest at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses torque with potential energy, which is extreme at 0° and 180°

quiz.q: An ideal electric dipole is one in which
options: the charges are equal to 1 C
the charges become infinite and the separation tends to zero, keeping p finite
the dipole has a net positive charge
quiz.explain: This limit gives a point dipole whose field formulas are exact at all r.
steps: The product p = q × 2a stays finite
Answer: the charges become infinite and the separation tends to zero, keeping p finite
quiz.mistake: Thinks ideal means a particular value of charge

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dipole in a uniform field may rotate but does not move bodily. Reason (R): The two forces on it are equal and opposite but do not act along the same line. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite forces with different lines of action form a couple: zero net force but non-zero torque.
steps: A: a dipole in a uniform field rotates but does not move bodily – true
R: the forces are equal and opposite but not along the same line – true
Such a couple gives zero net force but non-zero torque, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect a couple with rotation without translation

teach.ask: Gappu sees a paper bit jump to a charged comb. 'But paper is neutral! How?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The comb makes induced dipoles in the paper, and its non-uniform field pulls them. Neat!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens inside the neutral paper near the comb, and why does it matter that the field is not uniform?

revise.summary: In a uniform field a dipole feels zero net force but a torque τ = p × E (τ = pE sinθ) that aligns it with E. Polar molecules have permanent dipoles; non-polar ones get induced dipoles, and in non-uniform fields dipoles feel a net force.
focus: Net force and torque on a dipole
remember: τ = pE sinθ; maximum at 90°, zero at 0° and 180°
Polar: H₂O, HCl; non-polar: O₂, H₂, CO₂
traps: Zero net force does not mean zero torque
CO₂ is not polar: its bond moments cancel

learn.hook: Counting every electron on a charged wire is impossible. Instead, physicists use charge per metre, per square metre or per cubic metre, then let Gauss's law do the heavy lifting.
points: Linear charge density λ = charge per unit length (C m⁻¹), surface density σ = charge per unit area (C m⁻²), volume density ρ = charge per unit volume (C m⁻³).
For a continuous distribution, the total field is the integral (vector sum) of the fields of tiny elements: E = ∫ k dq r̂/r².
Charge is quantised, but over areas and volumes that hold billions of charges, averaging makes it look smooth, so densities make sense.
Gauss's law: the total electric flux through any closed surface = q_enclosed/ε₀.
Proof idea: for a charge q at the centre of a sphere of radius r, E = kq/r² everywhere on it, so flux = E × 4πr² = q/ε₀, the same for any radius or any closed shape enclosing q.

example.q: A point charge of 8.854 nC sits at the centre of a cube. What is the total flux through the cube? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
example.answer: 1000 N m² C⁻¹ (the cube's size does not matter)

learn.reallife: Engineers designing BHEL's high-voltage insulators estimate fields using charge densities and Gauss's law instead of tracking individual charges.

Outside charges give zero net flux.
Charge densities make sense only because charge is not quantised.
Charge is quantised; densities work by averaging over huge numbers of charges.
The SI unit of linear charge density is C m⁻¹.
Charge per metre.

quiz.q: A thin rod 50 cm long carries a uniform charge of 2 µC. What is its linear charge density (in µC m⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: λ = q/L = 2 µC/0.5 m = 4 µC m⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert cm to m

quiz.q: A charge of 17.708 nC lies inside a closed surface. What is the total flux through the surface (in N m² C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a factor of 10 with nano and pico

quiz.q: A point charge sits at the centre of a sphere. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the total flux through it
quiz.explain: Flux = q/ε₀ depends only on the enclosed charge.
steps: It does not depend on the radius of the sphere
quiz.mistake: Thinks a bigger surface catches more flux

quiz.q: Gauss's law states that the total flux through a closed surface equals
options: the net charge enclosed multiplied by ε₀
the net charge enclosed divided by ε₀
the total charge inside and outside divided by ε₀
the field multiplied by the charge
quiz.explain: φ = q_enc/ε₀ for any closed surface.
steps: Gauss's law: total flux through a closed surface = q_enc/ε₀
Answer: the net charge enclosed divided by ε₀
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by ε₀ instead of dividing

quiz.q: A metal sheet of area 2 m² carries a uniform charge of 6 µC. What is its surface charge density (in µC m⁻²)?
quiz.explain: σ = q/A = 6/2 = 3 µC m⁻².
quiz.mistake: Multiplies charge by area

quiz.q: In the proof of Gauss's law for a point charge at the centre of a sphere, why is E·dS simply E dS everywhere?
options: The field is zero on the sphere
The field is radial, so it is along the outward normal at every point of the sphere
The field is parallel to the surface
quiz.explain: By symmetry E is radial and the sphere's normal is radial, so the angle between them is zero.
steps: By symmetry the field of a central charge is radial
The sphere's outward normal is also radial, so the angle is 0 and E·dS = E dS
Answer: The field is radial, so it is along the outward normal at every point of the sphere
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sphere must be a conductor

quiz.q: Why can we use smooth charge densities even though charge is quantised?
options: Small elements still contain huge numbers of charges, so averaging gives a smooth density
quiz.explain: Macroscopic averaging over regions large compared with atomic sizes hides the graininess.
steps: Even tiny elements of a body contain huge numbers of charges
Averaging over them hides the graininess, giving smooth densities
Answer: Small elements still contain huge numbers of charges, so averaging gives a smooth density
quiz.mistake: Thinks densities contradict quantisation

quiz.q: The field of a continuous charge distribution is found by
options: treating the whole body as a point charge at its edge
dividing it into small elements dq and adding their fields as vectors (integration)
adding only the charges at the surface
multiplying the density by the distance
quiz.explain: Superposition extends to continuous charge by integration.
steps: Split the body into small elements dq, each like a point charge
Add their fields as vectors: E = ∫ k dq r̂/r²
Answer: dividing it into small elements dq and adding their fields as vectors (integration)
quiz.mistake: Treats an extended body as a single point at any distance

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a bigger balloon around a charge not catch more flux?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The field weakens as 1/r² exactly as the area grows as r², so flux is just enclosed charge over ε₀!
teach.nudge: Nearly! What does the flux depend on, and why does the surface size not matter?

revise.summary: Continuous charge is described by λ, σ and ρ, and its field is the vector integral of element fields. Gauss's law says the total flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀.
focus: Linear, surface and volume charge densities
Proof idea for a point charge
remember: λ = q/L, σ = q/A, ρ = q/V
Flux does not depend on the shape or size of the closed surface
traps: Charges outside do not add to net flux
Flux is q/ε₀, not qε₀

learn.hook: A charge sitting outside your Gaussian box is like a car driving straight through a toll plaza: it comes in one side and leaves the other, contributing nothing net.
points: A charge outside a closed surface sends as many lines in as out, so its net flux contribution is zero (though it still affects E at the surface).
Choose a Gaussian surface that matches the symmetry (sphere, cylinder, pillbox) so that E is constant and normal (or parallel) over each part.
A closed cube or cylinder in a uniform field has zero net flux: what enters one face leaves another.
Reverse use: if the flux through a closed surface is known from the field, the enclosed charge is q = ε₀φ.
A charge q at the centre of a cube sends q/6ε₀ through each face by symmetry.

example.q: A cube of side 0.1 m is in a field Ex = 50x N C⁻¹ (x in m), with faces at x = 0.1 m and x = 0.2 m. Find the net flux and the charge inside.
steps: Field is along x, so only the two faces normal to x carry flux.
example.answer: φ = 0.05 N m² C⁻¹ and q ≈ 4.4 × 10⁻¹³ C

learn.reallife: Signalling and data cables used by Indian Railways often have a metal sheath. Field lines from charges outside end on the sheath, so outside electric disturbances do not reach the wires inside.

games.title: Gaussian thinking
items: A charge just outside a closed surface contributes zero net flux through it.
Lines enter and leave.
If the net flux through a surface is zero, the field on the surface must be zero everywhere.
Only the net enclosed charge is zero; E can be non-zero.
A charge at the centre of a cube sends one sixth of its total flux through each face.
All six faces are symmetric.
A closed cylinder in a uniform field has zero net flux.
No charge is enclosed.
Gauss's law is useful only for spheres.
Any symmetric surface (cylinder, pillbox, sphere) can be used.

items: Cube in a uniform field
Sphere with +q inside
Box with +q and -q inside
Sphere with +2q outside it
Cylinder with -q on its axis inside
Box with +3q and -q inside

quiz.q: A point charge of 6 µC is at the centre of a cube. What is the flux through one face, in terms of 1/ε₀ (in µC)?
quiz.explain: Total flux 6 µC/ε₀ divides equally among 6 faces: 1 µC/ε₀ each.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to share the flux among six faces

quiz.q: A closed cylinder lies with its axis along a uniform electric field. The net flux through it is
options: E times the area of one end
quiz.explain: Flux enters one end and leaves the other; the curved surface has no flux; no charge is enclosed.
steps: The field is uniform: flux in through one end = flux out through the other
Curved surface is parallel to E: no flux; no charge enclosed
quiz.mistake: Counts only the outgoing flux

quiz.q: The net outward flux through a closed box is 8000 N m² C⁻¹. What charge (in nC) is inside? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
quiz.mistake: Divides φ by ε₀ instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Charges +3 µC, -5 µC are inside a closed surface and +10 µC is outside. The net flux is (in µC/ε₀)
quiz.explain: Only enclosed charges count: 3 - 5 = -2 µC, so φ = -2 µC/ε₀.
steps: Gauss's law counts only enclosed charges
q_enc = +3 − 5 = −2 µC (the +10 µC outside does not count)
quiz.mistake: Includes the outside charge

quiz.q: The net flux through a closed surface is zero. What can we conclude?
options: The net charge enclosed is zero
There is no charge anywhere nearby
The field on the surface is zero everywhere
The surface must be a sphere
quiz.explain: Zero flux means q_enc = 0; there may still be charges inside summing to zero, or charges outside.
steps: Charges may still exist inside (summing to zero) or outside
Answer: The net charge enclosed is zero
quiz.mistake: Concludes that E is zero on the surface

quiz.q: Why do we choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface for an infinitely long charged wire?
options: The wire's field is parallel to the curved surface
The field is radial and has the same magnitude at equal distances, matching a cylinder's symmetry
Spheres are not allowed for wires
quiz.explain: On the curved surface E is constant and along the normal; on the flat ends E is parallel to the surface, giving zero flux.
steps: A long wire's field is radial and equal at equal distances
A coaxial cylinder has E constant and normal on its curved face; ends give zero flux
Answer: The field is radial and has the same magnitude at equal distances, matching a cylinder's symmetry
quiz.mistake: Thinks any surface is equally convenient

quiz.q: A charge q is placed at one corner of a cube. What is the flux through the whole cube?
quiz.explain: Eight such cubes would surround the corner completely, so this cube gets one eighth of q/ε₀.
steps: Eight identical cubes meeting at that corner would enclose q fully
By symmetry each gets 1/8 of the total flux q/ε₀
quiz.mistake: Uses q/ε₀ without noticing only part of the charge's flux enters the cube

quiz.q: A field E = 3x î N C⁻¹ (x in m) exists. A cube of side 1 m has faces at x = 1 m and x = 2 m. What is the net flux through it (in N m² C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Out through x = 2: 6 × 1 = 6; in through x = 1: 3 × 1 = 3. Net = 6 - 3 = 3 N m² C⁻¹. Other faces are parallel to E.
quiz.mistake: Adds both faces or uses only one

teach.ask: Gappu put a charge outside his Gaussian box. 'Why is the flux zero if the field still pokes my box?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The outside charge's lines go in and come out, so only enclosed charge counts. Clever!
teach.nudge: Good thinking! What happens to each field line from an outside charge as it passes through the box?

revise.summary: Only enclosed charge contributes to net flux, so closed surfaces in uniform fields have zero flux. Gaussian surfaces are chosen to match symmetry, q = ε₀φ finds enclosed charge, and symmetry splits flux, e.g. q/6ε₀ per cube face.
focus: Flux from charges inside vs outside
remember: Charge at cube centre: q/6ε₀ per face; at a corner: q/8ε₀ through the cube
traps: Zero flux does not mean zero field on the surface
Don't count outside charges in q_enc

learn.hook: An overhead high-tension line is, to a nearby bird, almost an infinitely long charged wire. Gauss's law gives its field in two lines of algebra.
points: Infinitely long straight wire with uniform λ: Gaussian cylinder of radius r and length l gives E × 2πrl = λl/ε₀, so E = λ/(2πε₀r), radial and ∝ 1/r.
Infinite plane sheet with uniform σ: pillbox through the sheet gives 2EA = σA/ε₀, so E = σ/(2ε₀), normal to the sheet and independent of distance.
Two parallel plates with +σ and -σ: fields add between them to give σ/ε₀, and cancel outside to give zero.
These fields are directed away from positive charge and towards negative charge.
Real wires and sheets are finite, but the results hold well close to them and away from the edges.

example.q: An infinite line charge produces a field of 9 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ at 2 cm. Find λ.

learn.reallife: Electrostatic precipitators at Indian thermal power plants (like those of NTPC) use a charged central wire inside a tube. The strong λ/(2πε₀r) field near the wire charges smoke particles so they collect on the walls.

quiz.q: A long straight wire has λ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻¹. What is the field 10 cm from it (in N C⁻¹)? (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 in 2kλ/r

quiz.q: The field of an infinite line charge at 4 cm is 600 N C⁻¹. What is it at 12 cm (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: E ∝ 1/r for a line charge, so tripling r gives 600/3 = 200 N C⁻¹.
steps: r: 4 cm → 12 cm is 3 times larger
quiz.mistake: Uses 1/r² as for a point charge

quiz.q: An infinite plane sheet has σ = 17.708 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻². What is the field near it (in N C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses σ/ε₀, the result for a conductor or between plates

quiz.q: How does the field of an infinite plane sheet of charge change as you move away from it?
quiz.explain: E = σ/(2ε₀) has no r in it: the field lines are parallel.
steps: Field lines are parallel, so E stays constant
quiz.mistake: Applies a point-charge law to a sheet

quiz.q: Two large parallel plates carry σ = +8.854 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻² and -8.854 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻². What is the field between them (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Between the plates E = σ/ε₀ = 1 N C⁻¹.
steps: Between oppositely charged plates the fields add: E = σ/ε₀
quiz.mistake: Uses σ/2ε₀ for one sheet only

quiz.q: For the same pair of oppositely charged plates, what is the field outside them?
quiz.explain: Outside, the two sheet fields are equal and opposite, so they cancel.
steps: Outside, the +σ and −σ sheet fields are equal (σ/2ε₀) and opposite
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field leaks outside equally

quiz.q: In deriving E for an infinite line charge, why is there no flux through the flat ends of the Gaussian cylinder?
options: The radial field is parallel to the end faces, so E·dS = 0 there
The field is zero at the ends
quiz.explain: E is radial (perpendicular to the wire) and the end faces' normals are along the wire.
steps: The field of a line charge is radial, perpendicular to the wire
The end faces' normals are along the wire, so E ⟂ normal and E·dS = 0
Answer: The radial field is parallel to the end faces, so E·dS = 0 there
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ends contribute because they are part of the surface

quiz.q: Two infinite parallel sheets both carry the same positive σ. What is the field between them?
quiz.explain: Each sheet gives σ/2ε₀ pointing away from itself. Between them these point in opposite directions and cancel.
steps: Each positive sheet gives σ/2ε₀ pointing away from itself
Between them the two fields point in opposite directions
quiz.mistake: Copies the result for oppositely charged plates

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why doesn't a giant charged sheet get weaker as I fly away from it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The sheet's lines are parallel and never spread out, so E = σ/2ε₀ everywhere. Whoa!
teach.nudge: Almost! What do the field lines of a huge sheet look like, and why does that matter?

revise.summary: Gauss's law gives E = λ/(2πε₀r) for an infinite line charge and E = σ/(2ε₀) for an infinite sheet. Between oppositely charged parallel plates the field is σ/ε₀ and outside it is zero.
focus: Field of an infinite line charge
Field of an infinite plane sheet
remember: Sheet: E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of distance
Opposite plates: σ/ε₀ inside, 0 outside; like plates: 0 between
traps: Line field ∝ 1/r, not 1/r²
Sheet field is σ/2ε₀, not σ/ε₀

topics.title: Gauss's law: spherical shells and problem solving

learn.hook: Stand inside a hollow charged metal globe at a science fair and your hair stays flat. Gauss's law says the field inside is exactly zero.
points: Uniformly charged thin shell of radius R and charge q: outside (r > R) E = kq/r², as if all charge were at the centre.
Inside the shell (r < R) a Gaussian sphere encloses no charge, so E = 0 everywhere inside.
Just outside, E = kq/R² = σ/ε₀, where σ = q/4πR². The field jumps from 0 to σ/ε₀ across the shell.
Charge on a conductor from field: σ = ε₀E just outside, and q = σ × area.
Strategy: spot the symmetry, draw the Gaussian surface through the point, find q_enclosed, then solve for E.

example.q: A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm carries 1 nC. Find E at 5 cm and at 30 cm from the centre.

learn.reallife: Aircraft and Vande Bharat coaches act like metal shells: if lightning strikes, the charge stays on the outer skin and the field inside is close to zero, keeping passengers safe.

E = kq/r² contains only q and r.
The field inside a shell is zero only at its exact centre.
It is zero everywhere inside.

Choose a Gaussian surface through the point

quiz.q: A thin shell of radius 20 cm carries 4 nC. What is the field at 10 cm from its centre (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: 10 cm is inside the shell, where q_enc = 0, so E = 0.
steps: r = 10 cm < R = 20 cm, so the point is inside the shell
A Gaussian sphere there encloses no charge
quiz.mistake: Applies kq/r² inside the shell

quiz.q: For the same shell (4 nC, radius 20 cm), what is the field at 60 cm from the centre (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the shell radius instead of the distance from the centre

quiz.q: The field just outside a charged conductor is 8.854 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. What is the surface charge density (in µC m⁻²)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses σ = 2ε₀E, the sheet formula

quiz.q: A spherical conductor of radius 0.3 m has σ = 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². What is the field just outside it (in units of 10⁵ N C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
quiz.explain: E = σ/ε₀ = 10⁻⁶/8.854 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 1.13 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. The radius is not needed.
steps: Just outside a conductor: E = σ/ε₀ (radius not needed)
quiz.mistake: Uses σ/2ε₀ for a sheet

quiz.q: Which graph best describes E versus r for a charged thin spherical shell of radius R?
options: Rising linearly up to R then constant
Zero up to R, then a jump to a maximum at R, falling as 1/r² outside
Maximum at the centre, falling everywhere outward
quiz.explain: Inside E = 0; at R it jumps to kq/R²; outside it falls as 1/r².
steps: At r = R: jumps to kq/R²; outside: falls as 1/r²
Answer: Zero up to R, then a jump to a maximum at R, falling as 1/r² outside
quiz.mistake: Confuses the shell with a uniformly charged solid sphere

quiz.q: Why is the field outside a uniformly charged shell the same as that of a point charge at its centre?
options: A concentric Gaussian sphere outside encloses the full charge q and has the same symmetry as a point charge
Because the shell's charge moves to the centre
Because the shell is a conductor
Because the field inside is zero
quiz.explain: Gauss's law with spherical symmetry gives E·4πr² = q/ε₀ exactly as for a point charge.
steps: A concentric Gaussian sphere outside encloses all of q
Spherical symmetry gives E × 4πr² = q/ε₀, the point-charge result
Answer: A concentric Gaussian sphere outside encloses the full charge q and has the same symmetry as a point charge
quiz.mistake: Thinks charge physically moves to the centre

quiz.q: A charged shell's field at its outer surface is E₀. What is the field at a distance 2R from the centre?
quiz.explain: E ∝ 1/r² outside; going from R to 2R divides by 4.
steps: r: R → 2R, so E = E₀/2² = E₀/4
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 instead of 4

quiz.q: A thin plastic (insulating) spherical shell carries charge spread uniformly over it. A small charged bead is held at rest inside it, not touching. The force on the bead due to the shell's charge is
options: zero, because the field inside the shell is zero
directed towards the nearest point of the shell
quiz.explain: The uniformly spread charge on the shell produces no field anywhere inside it, so the bead feels no force from the shell.
steps: A Gaussian sphere inside the shell encloses none of the shell's charge
So the shell's field inside is zero and exerts no force on the bead
Answer: zero, because the field inside the shell is zero
quiz.mistake: Assumes the nearest part of the shell dominates

teach.ask: Gappu sits inside a charged hollow ball and asks: 'Why don't I feel any electric push?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A Gaussian sphere inside the shell encloses no charge, so the field is zero. I'm safe!
teach.nudge: Good! Draw a Gaussian sphere inside the shell. How much charge does it enclose?

revise.summary: For a uniformly charged thin shell, E = 0 inside and E = kq/r² outside, as if the charge were at the centre; just outside E = σ/ε₀. Use symmetry, a Gaussian surface and q_enc to solve problems.
focus: Field inside and outside a shell
remember: Just outside: E = σ/ε₀; σ = ε₀E
traps: Inside a shell the field is zero, not maximum
The radius is not needed for E = σ/ε₀
